ExpEvolve
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing
Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
Yongqiang Chen*†1,2, Chenxi Liu*3, Deyu Zou*4, Zhenhao Chen1, Tongliang Liu5,1, Bo Han3 and Kun Zhang1,2
1MBZUAI, 2Carnegie Mellon University, 3TMLR Group, Hong Kong Baptist University, 4The Chinese University of Hong Kong, 5SAIC
Centre, The University of Sydney
*Core contributors. †Project lead.
yqchen24@gmail.com
Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language
Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively
improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without
a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose
ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages
the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We
characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We
also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding
exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended
mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency
up to 5.0×. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from
MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration
and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.
1. Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used to build agents that operate on increasingly long-
horizon tasks (Plaat et al., 2025). One of the most ambitious applications is AI scientist agents (Zheng
et al., 2025a), in which LLMs automate the scientific discovery process, including literature sur-
veys (Asai et al., 2026), hypothesis generation (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), data-driven
analysis (Majumder et al., 2025), experiment design (Li et al., 2025a), or even the whole discov-
ery workflow (Gottweis et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2024; Mitchener et al., 2025; Yamada et al., 2025).
LLM-driven discovery has shown strong results in a variety of domains, such as mathematics (Ope-
nAI, 2026b,c), de novo protein design (Anthropic, 2026), algorithm discovery (Lange et al., 2026;
Novikov et al., 2025), and the research that develops LLMs themselves, an early form of recursive
self-improvement (RSI) (Favaro and Clark, 2026; Karpathy, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a; OpenAI, 2026a).
At the heart of the discovery loop is the iteration over scientific hypotheses, where scientific ideas
compound throughout the evaluation of promising hypotheses (Wallace et al., 2026). Therefore, it is
essential to reuse the discovery experience to generate high-quality hypotheses, e.g., avoiding getting
stuck in repetitive mistakes or suboptimal solutions and encoding promising exploratory proposals.
In this work, we study experience reuse in open-ended discovery with evolutionary coding agents,
where hypotheses are represented as solution programs to the underlying scientific problem, and expe-
riences are accumulated as evaluated programs and their scores given by an explicit evaluator (Novikov
et al., 2025). Typically, existing evolutionary coding agents such as ShinkaEvolve directly incorpo-
rate successful programs or rely on LLMs to summarize reusable insights and incorporate them as

Figure 1 | Comparison between experience reuse at program-level and idea-level. All programs solve
the same grid task. Left: Experience reuse at program-level is prone to low-level edits. Program-
level evolution derives new programs from a high-scoring parent, such as changing the heuristic
weight or bounding the search loop. Both edited programs score lower. Right: Experience reuse at
idea-level compares structurally different programs through a shared procedure-level factor, lp =
refine_lp(lp). Programs that contain the factor score higher than the program that omits it. This
contrast singles out the factor, which is then inserted into new programs of different structures.
memory for future mutations with LLMs (Gideoni et al., 2026; Karpathy, 2026; Lange et al., 2026).
However, program mutation contains an open-ended search space including low-level details such
as hyperparameters and high-level insights such as optimization strategies. LLM-driven guidance is
prone to focusing on low-level details (Karpathy, 2026; Pelleriti et al., 2026), which may not bring
genuine new scientific discoveries. In contrast, human scientists tend to recognize the high-level
contrasts among programs, accumulate and exploit scientific ideas from experience (Douven, 2025;
Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963). The gap raises a challenging research question:
How can we reuse experience for evolutionary discovery like human scientists?
To tackle the question, we formulate evolutionary discovery as a Partially Observable Markov
Decision Process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) (Sec. 3). In each turn, the agent needs to propose
meaningful solutions to uncover the underlying causal mechanism for solving the scientific problem,
i.e., maximizing the evaluation score (Glymour; Wallace, 1981). Under the formulation, we introduce
the notion of ideas as high-level mechanistic properties of the programs that determine the evaluation
scores, e.g., the construction family or the optimization strategy (Def. 3.2). Without uncovering the
ideas, the agent has to treat programs as unrelated and cannot tell whether a revision changes an idea
or only a low-level detail, so discovery degenerates into exhaustive search (Thm. 3.1). Meanwhile,
the identification of ideas also requires sufficient exploration to contrast programs with and without
each idea (Thm. 3.3). Hence, an effective discovery agent needs to extract ideas from experience,
and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary.
Motivated by the analysis, we propose ExpEvolve, which recognizes, structures, and leverages
the high-level idea factors from discovery experience (Fig. 1). Specifically, ExpEvolve realizes the
discovery of ideas via identifying high-level factors that help explain the program scoring differences.
Built upon COAT (Liu et al., 2025), the discovered idea factors are expected to predict which program
performs better given any pair of programs in the experience. Then, the admitted idea factors will be
incorporated as an action of a multi-armed bandit that controls the exploration and exploitation of
different ideas during discovery. To enable sufficient exploration, ExpEvolve also allocates slots for
random exploration (Gideoni et al., 2026), and idea-guided exploration when the evolution comes to
2


--- Page 3 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
a plateau. The idea-guided exploration enforces LLMs to explore diverse ideas other than those widely
used in top-scoring programs. The idea-based control in ExpEvolve allows efficient exploitation of
promising ideas while continuing to explore programs with varied ideas.
We evaluate ExpEvolve on 11 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks with a budget of 200
evaluated programs, using SCS as the backbone and the main baseline (Sec. 5). Under two con-
figurations that split the budget into 20 generations of 10 programs and 10 generations of 20
programs, ExpEvolve improves the final performance over SCS and ShinkaEvolve in most settings
with smaller budgets up to 5.0×. Further analyses show that the discovered idea factors order the
archived programs better than their code length on all 11 tasks. We further integrate ExpEvolve into
OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) on six tasks from MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a), where it improves
the mean final best-so-far score of OpenRSI on all six tasks.
2. Related Work
In this section, we discuss the closest related works and defer a more detailed one in Appendix B.
AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity and the development of
agentic systems, building LLM-based AI scientists has gained increasing attention (Zhou et al., 2025).
One research line automates part or the whole of the pipelines in scientific activities through agentic
workflows (Feng et al., 2026b; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Gottweis et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Lyu et al.,
2026b; Mitchener et al., 2025; Yamada et al., 2025). Evolutionary coding agents are one of the most
representative AI scientist agents that integrate LLMs into evolutionary search over programs scored by
an explicit evaluator (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). AI scientist agents, including
evolutionary coding agents, have made impact in a variety of domains, such as mathematics (OpenAI,
2026b), materials science (Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2025), biology (Anthropic, 2026), and the
development of LLMs themselves, e.g., accelerating LLM training and research toward recursive
self-improvement (Favaro and Clark, 2026; Karpathy, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a; OpenAI, 2026a;
Zhang et al., 2026). As generation scales up, validating the generated hypotheses becomes the main
cost (Wallace et al., 2026), and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed (Si et al.,
2026). The expanding paradigm of LLM-driven scientific discovery makes the reuse of experience
increasingly more essential, which is central to our work.
Experience reuse in evolutionary coding agents. Existing evolutionary coding agents typically
reuse experience via conditioning on evaluated programs (Gideoni et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025)
or summarizing textual insights from programs into memory for future mutations (Lange et al., 2026;
Liu et al., 2024; Volkov et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2024). The useful experience can also be exploited for
future search control, e.g., selection inspirations across diverse strategy clusters (Lange et al., 2026;
Luo et al., 2026). Different from existing works that concentrate on the unit of experience as texts or
programs, ExpEvolve discovers and exploits high-level idea factors to guide program mutations.
3. Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery
In this section, we formalize evolutionary discovery and introduce the notion of ideas.
3.1. Evolutionary Discovery as a POMDP
Scientific discovery aims to uncover the causal mechanisms underlying a problem through interactions
with the world (Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963). In evolutionary discovery, the agent interacts with the
problem through an evaluator. We denote by 𝜃sci ∈Θ the hidden mechanism of the problem, which is

builds the proposal context from its memory, e.g., parent and inspiration programs or summarized
insights, and generates candidate programs with an LLM 𝐺. The evaluator scores every program,
whose outcome depends on the hidden mechanism 𝜃sci, and the scored programs enter the archive
and update the memory. (B) The corresponding temporal graphical model. The memory 𝑚𝑡guides

and observes a score 𝑦𝑡with 𝔼[𝑦𝑡| 𝑝𝑡] = 𝐹(𝑝𝑡; 𝜃sci), where 𝐹: P × Θ →ℝis the objective, e.g., the
value of a mathematical construction, the efficiency of a kernel, or the performance of a trained
model (Novikov et al., 2025). The goal is to uncover 𝜃sci by optimizing for the evaluation score.
POMDP. As shown in Fig. 2B, the interaction forms a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process
(POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) with a static hidden state 𝑠𝑡= 𝜃sci, actions 𝑎𝑡= 𝑝𝑡, observations
𝑜𝑡= 𝑦𝑡, an identity transition kernel, and the observation kernel 𝑂(𝑦𝑡| 𝜃sci, 𝑝𝑡). Given a budget of 𝑇
evaluations, the agent chooses 𝑝0, . . . , 𝑝𝑇−1 to find a program ˆ𝑝with high 𝐹(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃sci).
Evaluation as intervention. 𝜃sci can be parameterized as a structural causal model over variables
of interest (Spirtes et al., 2000), in which a program specifies a configuration 𝑥𝑝of design variables 𝑋.
Each evaluation can be considered as the expected outcome of the intervention:

In this work, we leverage the causal view to provide a more in-depth understanding, while neither
the analysis nor the method requires recovering the causal graph. A full discussion on the relations
with causality can be found in Appendix C.
Experience-driven discovery. We define 𝑏𝑡as the agent’s Bayesian belief after accumulating
experience ℎ𝑡= {(𝑝0, 𝑦0), . . . , (𝑝𝑡−1, 𝑦𝑡−1)}, which is essentially a probability distribution on Θ, 𝑏𝑡(𝐵) =
Pr(Θsci ∈𝐵| ℎ𝑡) for 𝐵⊆Θ. In the ideal Bayesian formalism, the belief 𝑏𝑡is a sufficient statistic
for decision-making (Kaelbling et al., 1998). In practice, the AI Scientist maintains an internal
belief within LLMs, or an external one realized as memory 𝑚𝑡= Φ(ℎ𝑡) for some (possibly learnable)
summarization function Φ (Lange et al., 2026), to represent the approximate representation of its
knowledge about 𝜃sci and the landscape of 𝐹(·; 𝜃sci). Each evaluation step (𝑝𝑡, 𝑦𝑡) thus updates 𝑚𝑡,
which in turn updates the agent’s belief about 𝜃sci and determines the next action 𝑝𝑡+1.

3.2. Reusing Experience with Ideas
If the evaluator fully reveals 𝜃sci and the evaluation budget is unlimited, then enumerating every
possible program can directly lead to discovery. However, in reality, the evaluation score only reveals
partial information about 𝜃sci and evaluations can be expensive, e.g., training a model or running a
physical experiment, so the agent can afford only a limited number of them (Wallace et al., 2026).
Therefore, it is essential to reuse experience from past evaluations.
Without properly reusing experience, a single evaluation cannot reveal further insights about
other unseen programs, and the agent then has to evaluate every candidate program to find the best
one. Reusing experience requires some structure shared across programs, so that the evaluation of
one program also informs the others. We formalize the contrast as follows.
Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). Let P = {𝑝1, . . . , 𝑝𝐾}, and let each evaluation
return 𝑦𝑡= 𝐹(𝑝𝑡; 𝜃sci) + 𝜀𝑡with 𝜀𝑡∼N (0, 𝜎2) i.i.d.
(a) With reuse. If each program has a known representation 𝜙(𝑝) ∈ℝ𝑑with ∥𝜙(𝑝)∥2 ≤1 and
𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃sci) = ⟨𝜙(𝑝), 𝑤★⟩for an unknown 𝑤★∈ℝ𝑑, then under a coverage condition on the represen-
tation, there exists a policy that, with probability at least 1 −𝛿, outputs a program within 𝜖of the
optimal value after 𝑂␀𝑑𝜎2
𝜖2 log 𝐾
𝛿
 evaluations.
(b) Without reuse. If programs are unrelated, i.e., 𝐹(𝑝𝑖; 𝜃sci) = 𝜇𝑖for an arbitrary 𝜇∈ℝ𝐾, then any
policy with the same guarantee for every 𝜇needs Ω␀𝐾𝜎2
𝜖2 log 1
𝛿
 evaluations.
The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix E. Theorem 3.1 implies that reusing
experience at the high-level design choices can significantly improve sample efficiency from Ω(𝐾) to
𝑂(𝑑log 𝐾), where 𝐾≫𝑑. In evolutionary discovery, 𝐾counts the candidate program space, which
grow combinatorially with the high-level design choices and further with the ways of implementing
each choice, while 𝑑is determined by the design choices that affect the score. Most existing agents
retain experience at the level of programs (Lange et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025), which ignores
the high-level design choices. In contrast, human scientists recognize and record what they learn
from experiments in terms of reusable concepts, e.g., a construction or an optimization technique,
which carry over to later experiments. We are hence inspired to introduce the notion of ideas.
Definition 3.2 (Idea). An idea is an interpretable mapping 𝑧: P →V from programs to a binary
or categorical value. It describes a high-level mechanistic property that can be shared by syntactically
different programs, such as the construction family, initialization, or optimization procedure. A set of
ideas {𝑧1, . . . , 𝑧𝑟} defines the idea representation 𝑍(𝑝) = (𝑧1(𝑝), . . . , 𝑧𝑟(𝑝)).
A program realizes a set of ideas together with low-level details. We call an idea representation 𝑍
faithful if the score depends on a program only through its ideas, i.e., 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃sci) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝)) for some
function 𝑔determined by 𝜃sci. Under a faithful idea representation, the hidden mechanism acts on a
program only through its ideas, and Theorem 3.1 applies with 𝜙(𝑝) being the one-hot encoding of
𝑍(𝑝), whose dimension is determined by the number of ideas.
Identifiability of ideas. However, the agent does not know in advance which representation is
faithful, and the ideas have to be identified from the evaluated programs, while which programs are
evaluated is decided by the search itself. When the search stops varying the candidate ideas, the
exploration of ideas degenerates, as formalized below.
Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). Consider two candidate ideas 𝑧0 and 𝑧1, and
two mechanisms 𝜃0 and 𝜃1 under which the score depends on 𝑧0 and 𝑧1, respectively, i.e., 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) =
𝑔(𝑍(𝑝), 𝑧𝑖(𝑝)) for a common representation 𝑍and function 𝑔, with the same observation noise. Suppose
5

the optimal programs under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1 are different and unique with a margin Δ > 0. Then for any policy
that only evaluates programs on which 𝑧0 and 𝑧1 agree, there exists 𝑖∈{0, 1} such that for every budget
𝑇, the output ˆ𝑝satisfies 𝔼

max𝑝∈P 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) −𝐹(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃𝑖)

≥Δ/2.
The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix F. Theorem 3.3 can be considered as a
consequence of the partial observability of 𝜃sci, since the scores reveal 𝜃sci only through the evaluated
programs. If two candidate ideas agree on all explored programs, the two mechanisms produce the
same observations, and one cannot distinguish which idea determines the score. This situation is
common in evolutionary search: as the search concentrates around its current best programs, the
ideas shared by these programs stop varying. Identifying ideas thus requires sufficient exploration to
contrast programs with and without each idea, to isolate contributions of ideas in the program space.
4. ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience
Theoretical analysis in Sec. 3 suggests that a discovery agent should extract ideas from its experience,
and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary. We realize the theoretical principles in ExpEvolve.
The full procedure and implementation details are given in Alg. 1 and Appendix H.
4.1. Discovering Ideas from Experience
We leverage the discovery loop of the COAT framework (Liu et al., 2025) to find idea factors according
to their theoretical properties.

Figure 3 | Illustration of idea factor discovery.
Idea memory. During the discovery, ExpEvolve maintains an idea memory M𝑡which is a set of
idea factors. Each idea factor is stored with a name, a description of its code pattern, a type, i.e.,
binary or categorical, and a value set V. For each program in the experience archive, the values of
idea factors are annotated by an annotator LLM, which instantiates the idea representation 𝑍(𝑝).
Explainability of idea factors. A faithful idea representation is expected to be able to predict the
score of a program, i.e., 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃sci) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝)) (Sec. 3.2). However, predicting the exact scores from
ideas is difficult, since the scores of different tasks lie on different scales, the unknown function 𝑔can
be highly nonlinear, and the archive only contains a limited number of noisy evaluations. Therefore,
we define the explainability of an idea representation by its pairwise predictability, i.e., whether 𝑍(𝑝)
and 𝑍(𝑝′) predict which of two programs 𝑝and 𝑝′ is better. The ranking is already informative for
optimizing the objective, invariant to the scale of the scores, and more robust to noise than the scores.
6


--- Page 7 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
Discovering idea factors from unexplained pairs. The idea discovery process in ExpEvolve
is an iterative loop: each time the discovery is triggered, ExpEvolve fits a pairwise ranker on the
annotated idea factors, and selects the pairs of archived programs with a large score gap that the
current idea factors fail to explain. The unexplained pairs suggest the existence of missing idea factors
that separate the programs in each pair. For the selected pairs, a separate proposer LLM reads the
programs to propose candidate idea factors that distinguish them. Each candidate is then annotated
on the whole archive, and is admitted into the idea memory if each of its values is supported by
enough programs and its values separate the scores.

4.2. Exploiting Idea Factors for Discovery
We build a two-level exploration and exploitation framework with a multi-armed bandit (MAB) to
fully exploit discovered idea factors while exploring varying design spaces.
Exploration and MAB exploitation. In each generation, ExpEvolve keeps at least a fraction 𝜌
of the slots for random exploration that follows SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026) with randomly sampled
example programs, which explores programs beyond the current ideas and provides new material for
discovery. The remaining slots are allocated to idea-guided actions by MAB.

Figure 5 | Illustration of idea-guided exploration at plateaus.
Idea factors as MAB actions. To exploit an idea factor 𝑧, ExpEvolve compiles it into edit actions,
7


--- Page 8 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
e.g., ADD(𝑧) and REMOVE(𝑧) for a binary idea factor. An action adds to the context an instruction
that describes 𝑧, together with demonstration programs in the target state, to ask the mutator LLM to
realize the action in the new program. The MAB selects the action for each idea-guided slot. The
reward of an action is the score of the program generated under the action relative to the random
exploration in the same generation, i.e.,𝑟= 𝑦−¯𝑦rand
𝜎rand , where 𝑦is the score of the generated program,
and ¯𝑦rand and 𝜎rand are the mean and the standard deviation of the scores of random exploration
in the same generation. The normalization removes the drift of scores across generations and the
differences of score scales across tasks. The MAB selects the actions with an upper confidence bound
(UCB) rule on the maximum reward of each action (Appendix H.3).
Exploration at plateaus. Oftentimes, evolutionary discovery can concentrate around its best
programs and a single strategy. Consequently, the ideas widely used in top-scoring programs stop
varying, and their roles cannot be identified from the archive (Thm. 3.3). When the best score does
not improve for 𝜅generations, ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration, which enforces the
mutator LLM to explore diverse ideas other than those widely used in top-scoring programs. Specifi-
cally, a separate LLM probes the properties shared by the top-scoring programs as background idea
factors, and an LLM judge determines which idea factors in the memory depend on the background.
ExpEvolve then masks the actions of the dependent idea factors, instructs the mutator LLM to avoid
them, and assigns more slots to random exploration with diversified demonstrations.
5. Experiments
We evaluate ExpEvolve on 11 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks and further integrate it
into an evolutionary agent for Machine Learning Engineering (MLE) tasks.
5.1. Experimental Setup
Tasks. We evaluate on 11 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks. Nine tasks are the problems
studied by SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which are taken from AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025),
including the first and second autocorrelation inequalities, the uncertainty inequality, the Erdős
minimum overlap problem, sums and differences of sets, the max–min distance ratio, the Heilbronn
problem for triangles, the kissing number in 11 dimensions, and circle packing. The other two tasks
are the Hadamard matrix problem (Wang et al., 2026) and a variant of circle packing that recovers
the radii by linear programming. We report the best score at the end of the budget, as the mean and
standard deviation over seeds, and the best seed. Full details of the tasks are given in Appendix I.1.
Budget. Each run evaluates 200 programs. We consider two configurations with the same budget,
i.e., 10 generations of 20 programs as in SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026) and 20 generations of 10 programs,
which presents more challenges to accumulating reusable knowledge from experience.
Implementation. We compare ExpEvolve with SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which is the backbone
of ExpEvolve and shows competitive results against more elaborate evolutionary coding agents.
We further compare with ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), which maintains an island-based
archive and summarizes the insights of recent programs with a meta-summary. Details are given in
Appendix I.2. We use DeepSeek-V4-Flash by default, and each setting is run with 3 seeds. ExpEvolve
uses a random-exploration fraction 𝜌= 0.60 for 20-gen. and 𝜌= 0.40 for 10-gen. to keep a similar
number of random-exploration slots, i.e., 6 and 8. We donot tune other hyperparameters.

5.2. Main Results
ExpEvolve consistently improves the final performance. Table 1 shows the final performance at
the budget of 200 programs. ExpEvolve improves the mean and best final performances across most
settings over SCS and ShinkaEvolve. Moreover, the improvements are robust to how the budget
is parallelized. From 10 generations of 20 programs to 20 generations of 10 programs, the mean
final score of SCS can drop dramatically because of limited capability in experience reuse, while
ExpEvolve still maintains competitive performance. More details are given in Appendix J.

Figure 6 | Best-so-far scores along the budget of 200 evaluated programs.
ExpEvolve improves sample efficiency. Fig. 6 shows the best-so-far scores along the budget on
Hadamard, Sums and differences, Heilbronn, and Minimum overlap. On these four tasks, ExpEvolve
needs 1.7× to 26.2× fewer evaluations than SCS under both configurations.
The improvements transfer to other LLMs. Fig. 7 (a) shows that the advantages of ExpEvolve
over SCS transfers to other LLMs such as DeepSeek-v4-pro, GLM-5.2 and Gemini-3.7-Flash.
Summarizing experience as memory helps the early search but saturates. ShinkaEvolve and
SCS+meta retain the experience as a textual summary of recent programs, which provides additional
context to the mutator LLM without controlling which ideas are evaluated. Fig. 7 (b) shows that
SCS+meta improves over SCS in the early stage. However, its improvement slows down afterwards
while ExpEvolve keep improving. It again verifies the advantages of idea-guided evolution.
The discovered idea factors explain the order of archived programs. Following the definition
of explainability in Sec. 4.1, we measure the fraction of archived program pairs that discovered factors
can order correctly. As shown in Fig. 8(a), the discovered idea factors reach an accuracy of 0.79 to

programs come from idea-guided slots. The 92 idea-guided slots of the run select 7 distinct actions,
and all the new best programs from idea-guided slots come from 2 of them.
5.3. Additional Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering Tasks
We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to MLE by integrating it into
OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) and evaluating it on 6 tasks from MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a): Online
bandit, Anomaly detection, Clustering, Multi-objective optimization, Subgroup calibration shift, and
Evolution strategy. Search leverages the scores and execution feedback from each task.
Experimental setup. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which organizes search
through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators. For each task, we retain a fixed
history containing 20 completed search slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline
and OpenRSI equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50 additional evaluator
calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search slots per generation. All program generation uses
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve.

Figure 9 | Results on MLS-Bench. (a) Mean final scores. (b,c) Trajectories on two example tasks.
For each task and method, we average the final best-so-far (BSF) scores over three seeds.
Idea-guided evolution transfers to MLE tasks. Fig. 9(a) compares OpenRSI with OpenRSI+
ExpEvolve across the six tasks, where ExpEvolve shows superior performance on all six tasks, with
the largest gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.
Idea-guided actions produce better exploration and exploitation on MLE tasks. Fig. 9(b) and
Fig. 9(c) show two concrete trajectories in the tasks of multi-objective optimization and evolution
strategy, respectively. We can find that ExpEvolve can effectively discover useful ideas such as remov-
ing running ideal-point tracking (A1), removing reference-vector adaptation (A2), and adding hybrid
differential-evolution variation (A3) to effectively boost the performance. When the evolution gets
stuck at plateaus, exploiting useful strategies proposed by ExpEvolve in multi-objective optimization,
or exploration guided by idea factors in ExpEvolve can effectively break the plateaus and lead to
improvements. More details about the implementation can be found in Appendix K.1.
6. Conclusions
We introduced ExpEvolve, which structures the experience of evolutionary discovery into idea factors
and reuses them to guide the search. ExpEvolve discovers idea factors from the pairs of programs
that the current idea factors fail to explain, exploits them as the actions of a multi-armed bandit,
and keeps exploring programs where the ideas vary, through random exploration and idea-guided
exploration at plateaus. Our analysis shows that reusing a faithful idea representation reduces the
number of evaluations from Ω(𝐾) to 𝑂(𝑑log 𝐾), and that identifying ideas requires exploring programs
where the ideas vary. On 11 mathematical discovery tasks and 6 tasks from MLS-Bench, ExpEvolve
improves the final performance and the sample efficiency of evolutionary discovery under the same
evaluation budget.

ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
A. Limitations and Future directions
Due to the resource constraints, the tasks studied in this work remain limited to small-scale verification
and are relatively simple. There remains a broader scope of scientific problems to be explored where
verification signals can be expensive, such as biology, medicine, etc.. Meanwhile, the factor discovery
can also be guided with additional background knowledge of the task.
B. Related Work
In this section, we present more detailed discussions of related works in the literature.
AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity and the development
of agentic systems, a rising number of works develop agents to help scientific discovery (Tie et al.,
2025; Zheng et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025). Some systems automate the whole research workflow,
from idea generation to experimentation and paper writing (Feng et al., 2026b; Ghareeb et al.,
2026; Gottweis et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026b; Mitchener et al., 2025; Yamada et al.,
2025). One research line automates specific scientific activities, including literature review and deep
research (Asai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025b), hypothesis generation (Li et al., 2025c; Wang
et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024, 2025), hypothesis verification (Huang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2024),
and feedback on scientific papers (Liang et al., 2024). Another line targets data-driven discovery
and machine learning engineering (Chan et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2025; Majumder et al., 2025;
Wang et al., 2025c), as well as embodied agents in self-driving laboratories that conduct real-world
experiments (Mandal et al., 2025; Roch et al., 2020; Tom et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu et al.,
2022). A growing set of benchmarks evaluates the research abilities of these agents, e.g., replicating
and conducting AI research (Lyu et al., 2026a; Starace et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), generating
hypotheses from inspirations (Liu et al., 2026), discovering scientific laws and equations (Shojaee
et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2026), and conducting research tasks in biology (Laurent et al., 2024),
together with broader evaluations of research abilities (Wan et al., 2026). These lines of work
have made impact in mathematics (Bubeck et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2026b,c; Woodruff et al., 2026),
chemistry (Boiko et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2026a), materials science (Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2025),
earth science (Feng et al., 2026a), biology (Anthropic, 2026; Swanson et al., 2025; Truhn et al., 2026;
Wang et al., 2025a), and the development of LLMs themselves (Favaro and Clark, 2026; Karpathy,
2026; OpenAI, 2026a). As generation scales up, validating the generated hypotheses becomes the
main cost (Wallace et al., 2026), and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed (Si et al.,
2026), which motivates us to study how to reuse experience to reduce the evaluations needed in
evolutionary discovery.
Evolutionary coding agents. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) pairs an LLM with an
evaluator and a program database to discover new constructions in extremal combinatorics, and
AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) extends the loop to full codebases with an ensemble of LLMs,
with applications to a large set of mathematical problems (Georgiev et al., 2025). Follow-up frame-
works improve the search process: OpenEvolve provides an open-source implementation (Sharma,
2025); ShinkaEvolve improves sample efficiency with parent sampling, novelty rejection, bandit-
based LLM selection, and a meta-scratchpad that summarizes insights of recent programs (Lange
et al., 2026); CodeEvolve and GigaEvo maintain diversity with island models and quality-diversity
archives (Assumpção et al., 2025; Khrulkov et al., 2025); MCTS-AHD organizes heuristics in a Monte
Carlo search tree (Zheng et al., 2025b); and AdaEvolve adapts search intensity and resource alloca-
tion from the history of improvements (Cemri et al., 2026). The paradigm has also been applied to
equation discovery (Shojaee et al., 2025a) and systems research (Cheng et al., 2025). SCS shows
that simply conditioning on previous solutions is competitive with more elaborate pipelines (Gideoni
20


--- Page 21 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
et al., 2026), which we adopt as the backbone and main baseline. Classical evolutionary computation
also reuses experience through credit assignment over predefined units: adaptive operator selection
allocates budget across operators with multi-armed bandits (Da Costa et al., 2008), quality-diversity
methods maintain elites across behavior niches (Mouret and Clune, 2015) or search for novelty
alone (Lehman and Stanley, 2011), and MuEvo revises the priorities of heuristic components with
short-budget probing (Lv et al., 2026). In ExpEvolve, the units receiving credit are ideas discovered
during the search, and plateau handling targets the ideas shared by top programs.
Learned mutators and self-improving agents. Another line trains the LLM mutator with
reinforcement learning, either during evolution (Šurina et al., 2025) or at test time on a single
problem (Wang et al., 2026; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026), where experience is stored in model weights.
Self-improving agents such as the Darwin Gödel Machine and the Huxley-Gödel Machine evolve
the code of the agent itself (Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026), SATLUTION evolves a solver
repository together with its own rulebase (Yu et al., 2025a), and AlphaResearch alternates between
idea proposal and program verification (Yu et al., 2025b). These directions are orthogonal to ours,
which uses a fixed LLM and a fixed harness.
Causality for scientific discovery. There is a long history of discussions on how to understand
the world through observations (Greenland et al., 1999; Pearl, 2009; Spirtes et al., 2000). One
research line is causal discovery, which learns the causal structure among variables from observational
data under assumptions such as conditional independence or constrained functional forms (Hoyer
et al., 2008; Shimizu et al., 2006; Spirtes et al., 1995), from interventional data and data of multiple
domains (Brouillard et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Mooij et al., 2020; Perry et al., 2022; Yang et al.,
2018), and in the presence of latent variables (Li and Liu, 2025; Li et al., 2025d), while experiment
design selects the interventions that make the causal structure identifiable (Hyttinen et al., 2013; Li
et al., 2025a). Recently, LLMs have been used to construct structured variables out of unstructured
data (Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025), to estimate treatment effects from unstructured data (Dhawan
et al., 2024), and to propose instrumental variables (Sheth et al., 2025). Compared with these
works, the variables in ExpEvolve, i.e., ideas, are constructed from unstructured programs, and are
evaluated through interventions that the search itself chooses adaptively; Sec. 3.2 characterizes what
such an archive can identify.
C. A Causal View of the Formulation
In this section, we present a more detailed discussion of the causal view of evolutionary discovery in
Sec. 3.1.
C.1. Formulation of Scientific Discovery
Scientific discovery aims to uncover the underlying scientific knowledge or the causal mechanisms
from interactions with the world (Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963), which can be formulated as a Partially
Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) (Fig. 10).
Scientific knowledge.
The primary objective of an AI Scientist is to uncover the underlying scientific
knowledge about the task-world, represented by a latent variable Θsci ∈Θ, where Θ may encode causal
structure, mechanisms, inductive biases, constraints, etc. Specifically, Θsci = 𝜃sci can be parameterized
as a Structural Causal Model (SCM) 𝜃sci = (G, F , 𝑃𝑈) (Spirtes et al., 2000), where G = (𝑉, 𝐸) is
a directed graph whose nodes 𝑉represent variables of interest and whose edges 𝐸encode direct
causal dependencies; F = { 𝑓𝑣}𝑣∈𝑉is a collection of structural equations 𝑣= 𝑓𝑣(Pa(𝑣), 𝑢𝑣), where Pa(𝑣)

𝑚𝑡+1. Over time steps 𝑡, 𝑡+ 1, . . . , this recurrent process allows the agent to navigate the performance
landscape and converge towards optimal programs despite the static but unknown nature of 𝜃sci.

Evaluation as intervention on SCM.
Given the SCM parametrization of 𝜃sci, we can consider that a
program 𝑝∈P is encoded as a particular configuration of design variables 𝑋= 𝑥𝑝. Then, 𝐹can be
implemented as
𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃sci) := 𝔼

𝑌
 do(𝑋= 𝑥𝑝), 𝜃sci

,
i.e., the expected outcome under the intervention do(𝑋= 𝑥𝑝) in the true causal model 𝜃sci. Typical
implementations of 𝐹can be the objective value of a combinatorial optimization problem, the efficiency
of a kernel program, or the performance of a machine learning model (Novikov et al., 2025).
Belief as revealed knowledge.
As in Sec. 3.1, the AI Scientist maintains a memory 𝑚𝑡= Φ(ℎ𝑡) as
an approximate belief about 𝜃sci. Each evaluation step (𝑝𝑡, 𝑦𝑡) thus updates 𝑚𝑡, which in turn updates
the agent’s effective belief about 𝜃sci. In this sense, each step reveals part of the underlying scientific
knowledge, which in turn determines the next action 𝑝𝑡+1.
C.2. Ideas and Causal Representation Learning
Ideas as high-level causal variables.
In the SCM view above, a program specifies a configuration 𝑥𝑝
of design variables 𝑋, which are low-level and high-dimensional, e.g., every line of the code. An idea 𝑧
(Definition 3.2) is a function of the program, and hence of 𝑥𝑝, that summarizes the design variables at
a higher level. A faithful idea representation (Sec. 3.2) requires that 𝔼[𝑌| do(𝑋= 𝑥𝑝), 𝜃sci] depends
22


--- Page 23 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
on 𝑥𝑝only through 𝑍(𝑝), i.e., interventions on the design variables that keep all ideas fixed leave
the expected outcome unchanged. Hence, an intervention on the ideas is well defined at the level
of expected outcomes. This condition is related to causal feature learning (Chalupka et al., 2015),
which constructs macro-level causal variables by grouping the micro-level states that induce the same
outcome distribution under intervention, and to causal abstraction (Rubenstein et al., 2017), which
studies when a high-level causal model is consistent with a low-level one. Faithfulness is a mean-level
version of these conditions, restricted to the score of interest.
Relation to causal representation learning.
Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to recover
high-level causal variables from low-level observations (Schölkopf et al., 2021), where identifiability
usually relies on additional information such as interventions on the latent variables (Ahuja et al.,
2023). Ideas can be viewed as the high-level causal variables of programs, and the two settings differ
in three aspects. (i) In CRL, the representation is usually an encoder learned from the observations,
while an idea is an interpretable function of the program that an LLM can annotate, similar to how
LLMs construct high-level variables from unstructured data (Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025). (ii)
CRL usually aims to recover all latent variables, while ideas only need to be faithful to the score. (iii)
The agent decides which programs to evaluate, and an edit that changes one idea and keeps the
others fixed acts as an intervention on that idea, although an LLM edit may also change other ideas.
Theorem 3.3 shows that when the evaluated programs do not vary the candidate ideas, the ideas that
matter cannot be identified from the scores.
C.3. Essentiality of Causal Knowledge for AI Scientists
If the evaluation revealed the scientific knowledge completely, then with more experiment turns,
the agent’s revealed scientific knowledge would converge to 𝜃sci. However, the observation from
the evaluation is usually only a proxy of the scientific knowledge Θsci: each evaluation returns a
scalar score of the program that the agent chooses to evaluate. Different hypotheses about 𝜃sci, e.g.,
ones under which different ideas determine the score, can produce the same scores on all evaluated
programs. For example, if all evaluated programs in circle packing share the same initialization and
the same refinement, the scores cannot tell which of the two accounts for the performance. Therefore,
the causal knowledge often cannot be identified from the scores of the programs explored so far, and
it is essential for an AI Scientist to explore sufficiently, i.e., to evaluate programs that distinguish the
competing hypotheses. We denote by 𝑒src the environment in which the evaluation is conducted.
Definition C.1 (Causal AI Scientist). A Causal AI Scientist is an agent specified by: (i) a policy
𝜋𝑡(· | 𝜃𝑡, 𝑒src) selecting 𝑝𝑡, (ii) a counterfactual / explanatory operator CF, that answer interventional
queries (𝑒, 𝑝) via CF(𝜃𝑡; 𝑒, 𝑝) as an “explanation” of predicted performance, where 𝜃𝑡is the knowledge
revealed at turn 𝑡.
Without the revealing of the causal knowledge, the discovery process suffers from significant
inefficiency and suboptimality issues. We discuss the two issues more concretely below.
Evolutionary efficiency of Causal AI Scientist. The efficiency issue is characterized by Theo-
rem 3.1. In the linear setting of Theorem 3.1, a Causal AI Scientist can be implemented via estimating
the 𝑤★and optimizing for ˆ𝑝from the history, while the black-box baseline does not consider the
interactions between the historical observations. Theorem 3.1 shows that, when 𝐾≫𝑑, which is
usually the case as the space for all programs is significantly larger than the underlying SCM, encod-
ing (correct) causal structure, e.g., a faithful idea representation, yields an exponential (or at least
multiplicative) gain in sample efficiency under finite budgets. For example, if 𝐾grows exponentially
23

ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
with 𝑑, e.g., 𝐾= 2𝑑, the upper bound in Theorem 3.1 grows polynomially in 𝑑, as 𝑂␀𝑑(𝑑+ log 1
𝛿) 𝜎2

while the lower bound for the black-box baseline grows exponentially in 𝑑, as Ω␀2𝑑log 1

Sufficient exploration of Causal AI Scientist. The suboptimality issue is characterized by
Theorem 3.3. Let 𝑆⊆P be the set of programs evaluated by the agent. Two hypotheses 𝜃0 and
𝜃1 can be distinguished from the history only if their observation models differ on some program
in 𝑆; otherwise, the history has the same distribution under both hypotheses. Under the idea-level
mechanisms in Theorem 3.3, i.e., 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝), 𝑧𝑖(𝑝)) for 𝑖∈{0, 1}, the two hypotheses agree
on every program where 𝑧0 and 𝑧1 agree, so only the programs where the two ideas differ can
distinguish them. Intuitively, Theorem 3.3 implies that if the evaluated programs do not distinguish
the corresponding 𝜃sci among {𝜃0, 𝜃1}, then the solution ˆ𝑝incurs an expected regret of at least Δ/2
under one of them, regardless of the budget. This situation is common in evolutionary search: as
the search concentrates around its current best programs, the ideas shared by these programs stop
varying among the evaluated programs, and the scores cannot tell whether these ideas are the ones
that matter. Hence, a Causal AI Scientist needs to explore the programs in which the competing ideas
differ, so that the scores can distinguish the hypotheses. This barrier can be removed by exploration
within the same evaluator, which differs from the transfer across environments discussed below.
C.4. Transfer of Scientific Knowledge across Environments
Beyond a single evaluator, the revealed scientific knowledge is also expected to transfer to other
environments. If the objective function 𝐹is static universally, then with more experiment turns, the
optimized solution 𝑝𝑡and the agent’s revealed scientific knowledge can also be applied universally.
However, the evaluation is usually conducted at some specific environment 𝑒∈E, which only gives a
proxy knowledge 𝜃𝑒about the scientific knowledge Θsci. For example, the performance of a machine
learning model is usually assessed on finite samples from the test distribution, and there also exist
distribution shifts from the test distribution when deploying the model in the real world (Quinonero-
Candela et al., 2008). Different from Θsci that characterizes the complete causal structure about the
scientific problem, optimization under environment 𝜃𝑒may introduce some spurious correlations
that maximize the objective value 𝐹𝑒(Chen et al., 2023). Therefore, to retain the optimality of ˆ𝑝
beyond the source environment 𝑒src to some target 𝑒tgt, it is essential to reveal the causal knowledge
and answer causal questions for an AI Scientist, e.g., through the operator CF in Definition C.1. Let
𝑃𝑒(· | 𝑝, 𝜃) denote the observation model of the evaluator in environment 𝑒, with mean 𝐹𝑒(𝑝; 𝜃). We
have the following:
Theorem C.2. Consider 𝑒src, 𝑒tgt ∈E and 𝜃0, 𝜃1 ∈Θ such that 𝑃𝑒src(· | 𝑝, 𝜃0) = 𝑃𝑒src(· | 𝑝, 𝜃1) for all
𝑝∈P, and the optimal programs in 𝑒tgt under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1 are different and unique, each better than all
other programs by at least Δ > 0. Then for any policy 𝜋that can interact only with 𝑒src, there exists
𝑖∈{0, 1} such that for every budget 𝑇, 𝔼

max𝑝∈P 𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) −𝐹𝑒tgt(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃𝑖)

≥Δ/2.
The formal description and the proof are given in Appendix G. Intuitively, Theorem C.2 implies
that if the source environment does not distinguish the corresponding 𝜃sci among {𝜃0, 𝜃1}, then the
solution ˆ𝑝solved given source environment is suboptimal in the target environment under one of
them, no matter how many evaluations are made in the source environment. In the real world, it is
usually the case that two machine learning models will have similar performances under the public
test benchmarks, but exhibit significantly different behaviors when generalizing to distributions from
other environments. Different from Theorem 3.3, this barrier cannot be removed by more exploration
in the source environment, since the two hypotheses agree on every program there. We leave a full
study of the transfer of scientific knowledge across environments to future work.

D.2. Random variable, space, and realization (to avoid notation confusion)
We use the following (standard) convention.
(i) Hypothesis space. Θ is a set that contains all candidate scientific-knowledge hypotheses.
(ii) True but unknown instance. The real world is governed by a fixed but unknown 𝜃★∈Θ.
(iii) Bayesian view (optional but convenient). A Bayesian agent models uncertainty by treating
𝜃★as a realization of a latent random variable Θsci with prior 𝜇0, i.e. Θsci ∼𝜇0 and 𝜃★is one draw
from it. The belief 𝑏𝑡is simply the posterior distribution of Θsci after seeing history ℎ𝑡.
(iv) Does scientific knowledge change across environments? In our formulation, the underlying
scientific knowledge 𝜃★is static across rounds. Different environments 𝑒∈E represent different
evaluation/deployment protocols (distribution shifts, constraint changes, measurement noise, private
vs public tests, etc.). Formally, environments affect either the true performance map 𝐹𝑒(·; 𝜃) and/or
the observation kernel 𝑃𝑒(· | 𝑝, 𝜃), while 𝜃★itself remains the same hidden instance.
D.3. Evaluator as an observation model (covers deterministic and stochastic evaluators)
Fix an environment 𝑒∈E. When the agent evaluates program 𝑝, it receives an observation 𝑦∈Y
drawn from
𝑦∼𝑃𝑒(· | 𝑝, 𝜃★),

E. Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse)
Throughout this section we fix a single static environment (drop 𝑒from notation), and assume
P = {𝑝1, . . . , 𝑝𝐾} is finite.

E.1. Protocol and performance criterion
Experiment–then–commit protocol.
A policy 𝜋interacts for 𝑇rounds. At each round 𝑡= 0, . . . , 𝑇−1
it selects a program 𝑝𝑡∈P (possibly randomized) based on the past history ℎ𝑡, then observes 𝑦𝑡∈ℝ.
After 𝑇evaluations it outputs a final recommendation ˆ𝑝∈P.
Simple regret.
Let 𝑓(𝑝) denote the true mean performance of program 𝑝in this environment.
Define the (random) simple regret
SR𝑇:= max
𝑝∈P 𝑓(𝑝) −𝑓(ˆ𝑝).
(3)
(𝜖, 𝛿)-correctness (uniform).
Fix 𝜖> 0 and 𝛿∈(0, 1). We say a policy 𝜋is (𝜖, 𝛿)-correct uniformly
on a hypothesis class H if for every instance in H,
Pr ␀SR𝑇≤𝜖 ≥1 −𝛿.
“Uniformly” means the guarantee must hold for all instances in the class, not only on average.
E.2. Two hypothesis classes
(1) Structured class. Each program 𝑝has a known representation 𝜙(𝑝) ∈ℝ𝑑with ∥𝜙(𝑝)∥2 ≤1, e.g.,
a faithful linear idea representation 𝜙(𝑝) = 𝑍(𝑝) (Sec. 3.2). The unknown instance is a weight vector
𝑤★∈ℝ𝑑and
𝑓(𝑝) = ⟨𝜙(𝑝), 𝑤★⟩.
(4)

𝜀𝑡∼N (0, 𝜎2) i.i.d.

(2) Unstructured black-box class (baseline). The unknown instance is an arbitrary vector of

Remark (deterministic evaluator).
If 𝜎= 0, the structured linear class can recover 𝑤★exactly
from 𝑑basis evaluations and achieve SR𝑇= 0, while in the unstructured black-box class a uniform

Relation to best-arm identification.
The lower bound follows the standard change-of-measure
argument for best-arm identification in 𝐾-armed Gaussian bandits (Kaufmann et al., 2016), and the
upper bound is a simple instance of best-arm identification in linear bandits (Soare et al., 2014).
F. Proof of Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas)
F.1. Formal statement and proof
For a policy that interacts for 𝑇rounds and outputs ˆ𝑝, define the simple regret under mechanism 𝜃as
SR𝑇(𝜃) := max𝑝∈P 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃) −𝐹(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃).
Theorem F.1 (Formal version of Theorem 3.3). Let 𝑧0, 𝑧1 : P →V be two ideas, and let 𝐴:= {𝑝∈P :
𝑧0(𝑝) = 𝑧1(𝑝)} be the set of programs on which they agree. Assume there exist 𝜃0, 𝜃1 ∈Θ such that:
(i) (Idea-level mechanisms) 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝), 𝑧𝑖(𝑝)) for all 𝑝∈P and 𝑖∈{0, 1}, for a common
representation 𝑍and function 𝑔, and each evaluation returns 𝑦= 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) + 𝜀with the same noise
distribution under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1;
(ii) (Optimal program flips with margin Δ) there exist 𝑝0 ≠𝑝1 and Δ > 0 such that 𝐹(𝑝𝑖; 𝜃𝑖) −
𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃𝑖) ≥Δ for all 𝑝≠𝑝𝑖and 𝑖∈{0, 1}.
Then for any policy that only evaluates programs in 𝐴, there exists 𝑖∈{0, 1} such that for every budget 𝑇,
𝔼

SR𝑇(𝜃𝑖)

≥Δ/2.
Moreover, at least one of 𝑝0 and 𝑝1 lies outside 𝐴.
Proof. For every 𝑝∈𝐴, 𝑧0(𝑝) = 𝑧1(𝑝) gives 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃0) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝), 𝑧0(𝑝)) = 𝑔(𝑍(𝑝), 𝑧1(𝑝)) = 𝐹(𝑝; 𝜃1).
Together with the common noise distribution in (i), the observation model 𝑂(· | 𝜃𝑖, 𝑝) is identical
under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1 for every 𝑝∈𝐴.
Let ℙ𝑖be the distribution of the transcript (𝑝0:𝑇−1, 𝑦0:𝑇−1, ˆ𝑝) when the true mechanism is 𝜃𝑖. Since
the policy only evaluates programs in 𝐴, for any history and any chosen 𝑝𝑡∈𝐴, the conditional
distribution of 𝑦𝑡is identical under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1, and the policy chooses 𝑝𝑡+1 and ˆ𝑝with the same
randomization given the same history. By induction on 𝑡, ℙ0 = ℙ1. In particular, the output ˆ𝑝has the
same distribution 𝑄on P under both mechanisms.
By (ii), any output ˆ𝑝≠𝑝𝑖incurs regret at least Δ under 𝜃𝑖, so
𝔼[SR𝑇(𝜃0)] ≥Δ ␀1 −𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝0)
,
𝔼[SR𝑇(𝜃1)] ≥Δ ␀1 −𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝1)
.
Since 𝑝0 ≠𝑝1, 𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝0) + 𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝1) ≤1, so at least one of the two probabilities is at most 1/2, and
the corresponding expected regret is at least Δ/2.
For the last claim, suppose both 𝑝0, 𝑝1 ∈𝐴. Then 𝐹(𝑝1; 𝜃0) = 𝐹(𝑝1; 𝜃1) ≥𝐹(𝑝0; 𝜃1) + Δ =
𝐹(𝑝0; 𝜃0) + Δ, which contradicts the optimality of 𝑝0 under 𝜃0.
□

The theorem holds for any budget, since the barrier comes from the programs that the policy
evaluates. To identify which of 𝑧0 and 𝑧1 matters, the policy has to evaluate a program outside 𝐴, i.e.,
a program on which the two ideas differ. In ExpEvolve, this is the role of plateau-aware revision,
which changes the proposal distribution to evaluate programs where the ideas shared by the leading
programs differ.
G. Proof of Theorem C.2 (Non-identifiability under environment shifts)
G.1. Setup: source interaction, target evaluation, and target regret
The agent can only interact with the source environment 𝑒src:
𝑦𝑡∼𝑃𝑒src(· | 𝑝𝑡, 𝜃★).
After 𝑇rounds it outputs a final program ˆ𝑝. Performance is judged in a target environment 𝑒tgt via
𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃★). Define the target (simple) regret:
GR𝑇(𝜃★) := max
𝑝∈P 𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃★) −𝐹𝑒tgt(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃★).
G.2. Formal statement and proof
Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). Fix 𝑒src, 𝑒tgt ∈E. Assume there exist two
hypotheses 𝜃0, 𝜃1 ∈Θ such that:
(Source indistinguishability)
𝑃𝑒src(· | 𝑝, 𝜃0) = 𝑃𝑒src(· | 𝑝, 𝜃1),
∀𝑝∈P.
(10)
(Target optimal action flips with margin Δ)
∃𝑝0, 𝑝1 ∈P and Δ > 0 s.t.
(11)
𝑝0 ∈arg max
𝑝∈P 𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃0),
𝑝1 ∈arg max
𝑝∈P 𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃1),
𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝0; 𝜃0) −𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃0) ≥Δ, ∀𝑝≠𝑝0,
𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝1; 𝜃1) −𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝; 𝜃1) ≥Δ, ∀𝑝≠𝑝1.
(12)
Then for any policy 𝜋that can interact only with 𝑒src, there exists 𝑖∈{0, 1} such that for every budget
𝑇,
𝔼

GR𝑇(𝜃𝑖)

≥Δ/2.
This impossibility holds whether the evaluator is stochastic or deterministic, since equation 10 is stated
at the level of the full observation model 𝑃𝑒src.
Proof. Let ℙ𝑖be the distribution over the full transcript
T := (𝑝0:𝑇−1, 𝑦0:𝑇−1, ˆ𝑝)
when the true hypothesis is 𝜃𝑖and interaction is only with 𝑒src.
By equation 10, for any history and any chosen action 𝑝𝑡, the conditional distribution of 𝑦𝑡is
identical under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1. By induction on 𝑡, the entire transcript distribution is identical:
ℙ0 = ℙ1.
In particular, the marginal distribution of the final output ˆ𝑝is the same under 𝜃0 and 𝜃1. Let this
common distribution be denoted by 𝑄on P.

--- Page 32 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
Now consider the expected target regret under 𝜃0: by equation 12, any output ˆ𝑝≠𝑝0 incurs
regret at least Δ under 𝜃0:
GR𝑇(𝜃0) = 𝐹𝑒tgt(𝑝0; 𝜃0) −𝐹𝑒tgt(ˆ𝑝; 𝜃0) ≥Δ · 1{ˆ𝑝≠𝑝0}.
Taking expectation w.r.t. 𝑄yields
𝔼[GR𝑇(𝜃0)] ≥Δ · (1 −𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝0)).
Similarly,
𝔼[GR𝑇(𝜃1)] ≥Δ · (1 −𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝1)).
Since 𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝0) + 𝑄(ˆ𝑝= 𝑝1) ≤1, at least one of these probabilities is at most 1/2, so at least one of
the two expected regrets is at least Δ/2:
max{𝔼[GR𝑇(𝜃0)], 𝔼[GR𝑇(𝜃1)]} ≥Δ/2.
This proves the claim.
□
G.3. Concrete examples satisfying the conditions
We give two illustrative examples where source data cannot distinguish two hypotheses, yet the
target-optimal decision differs.
Example 1: public test vs private (distribution shift / shortcut feature).
Let 𝜃∈{𝜃0, 𝜃1} encode
which feature is truly stable/causal. Programs correspond to two model families: 𝑝0 uses a stable
causal feature; 𝑝1 uses a shortcut feature. In the source environment (public benchmark), the shortcut
feature is perfectly correlated with labels, so both hypotheses yield the same evaluator distribution for
every program, satisfying equation 10. In the target environment (deployment/private), the shortcut
correlation breaks: under 𝜃0, 𝑝0 is uniquely optimal; under 𝜃1, 𝑝1 is uniquely optimal, with margin Δ,
satisfying equation 12. No amount of interaction with 𝑒src can identify which world holds.
Example 2: relaxed verification (slack) vs exact verification (constraint shift).
In combinatorial
optimization, it is common to evaluate candidate programs using a relaxed verifier (e.g., allowing
numerical slack), then validate with an exact verifier. For instance, in circle packing, one may verify
non-overlap with a numerical slack such as 10−6, and later validate with an exact checker; converting
a relaxed-feasible solution into an exact-feasible one may require tiny but nonzero modifications, and
rankings can change when switching verifiers. This is explicitly discussed in the context of circle
packing verification with slack vs exact validation. The source environment 𝑒src can correspond to the
relaxed evaluator, while the target environment 𝑒tgt corresponds to the exact evaluator. Then two
hypotheses 𝜃0, 𝜃1 can be constructed so that they are indistinguishable under the relaxed evaluator
for all queried programs, yet the exact evaluator reverses which program is truly best (with gap Δ),
matching Theorem G.1.
H. Implementation Details of ExpEvolve
This section describes the implementation of ExpEvolve used in our experiments. Alg. 1 summarizes
the search loop, and Alg. 2 details the discovery of idea factors. We implement ExpEvolve on the
backbone of SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026). In each generation, ExpEvolve generates 𝐵programs in
parallel slots. The prompt of each slot contains the task instruction, an optional strategy instruction

from an idea-guided action, a summary of the idea memory, and a few example programs, and the
mutator LLM 𝐺writes a new program from the prompt. All LLM calls use DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and
the hyperparameters are listed in Table 3. Each generated program is evaluated once. A program
is treated as failed if the evaluation fails or returns a non-finite objective, and failed programs are
neither repaired nor retried. The LLM calls for generation are not retried in our experiments either,
so a failed call, e.g., due to rate limits, yields a failed program that still counts toward the evaluation
budget.
H.1. Idea Memory and Annotation
Idea factors. Each idea factor 𝑧in the idea memory M𝑡is stored with a name, a description of its
code pattern, a type, i.e., binary or categorical, and a value set V. The description is also used by
the annotator LLM to recognize the idea factor from the source code. The annotator LLM labels
each program with 𝑧(𝑝) ∈V ∪{unknown}, where the label is unknown if the idea factor cannot be
recognized. The annotation of a program is a separate LLM call, independent of the proposal of idea
factors, with the source code truncated to 4000 characters.
Score contrast. For a binary idea factor, the score contrast is the difference of the mean scores
between the successful programs labeled true and those labeled false. For a categorical idea factor,
the score contrast is the difference of the mean scores between the value with the highest mean score
and the value with the lowest mean score. Programs labeled unknown are excluded from the score
contrast.
Updating the memory. After each generation, UpdateMemory labels the new programs with
all existing idea factors, recomputes the score contrasts, and merges two idea factors if the Pearson
correlation of their labels on the archive exceeds 0.85 (Alg. 1, line 8). Degenerate evaluations, whose
scores collapse to extreme values, are excluded from the statistics. It also updates the statistics of the
actions (Appendix H.3).
33


--- Page 34 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery

Ensure: updated idea memory M
Select unexplained contrasts
1: if M = ∅then
2:
𝑄←LargestScoreGaps(A, ℓ)
3: else
4:
𝑄←MisrankedPairs(A, M, ℓ) {pairwise ranker on 𝑍(𝑝)}
5: end if
Propose candidate ideas
6: f
M ←ProposeIdeas(𝑄) {name, description, type, values}
Annotate, test, and admit
7: for each 𝑧∈f
M do
8:
𝑧(𝑝) ←Annotate(𝑝, 𝑧) for all 𝑝∈A {in V ∪{unknown}}
9:
if Supported(𝑧, A, 𝑛min) and |ScoreContrast(𝑧, A)| ≥𝜂and not Duplicate(𝑧, M) then
10:
M ←M ∪{𝑧}
11:
end if
12: end for
13: return M
Memory summary in the prompt. Every slot, including random exploration, receives a summary
of the idea memory (line 5). The summary lists the six idea factors with the largest absolute score
contrasts, each with its name, description, direction of effect, numbers of programs with and without
it, and score contrast, and gives the mean score of each value for categorical idea factors. It also
contains the outlier programs that the current idea factors fail to explain, i.e., one program with
a large positive residual and one with a large negative residual (|𝑧| ≥1.5), with their source code
truncated to 1500 characters.
H.2. Idea Discovery
Trigger. Discovery is triggered every 𝑛disc generations after the first generation, when the archive
contains at least 15 successful programs and the idea memory contains fewer than 12 idea factors,
excluding the background idea factors (Alg. 1, line 9).
Pairwise ranker. Let 𝜎𝑌be the standard deviation of the scores of the successful programs in the
archive. ExpEvolve builds all pairs of successful programs (𝑝, 𝑝′) with |𝑦(𝑝) −𝑦(𝑝′)| ≥0.25 𝜎𝑌, and
labels each pair by sign(𝑦(𝑝) −𝑦(𝑝′)). The feature of a pair is the difference of the binary encodings
of the idea factors, where a factor is encoded as 1 if it is labeled true and 0 otherwise, together with
the standardized difference of the code lengths as a covariate. The ranker is a ridge least-squares
model without intercept (𝜆= 10−3), refit in each discovery round.
Selecting unexplained pairs. ExpEvolve selects the pairs that the ranker orders incorrectly
(Alg. 2, line 4), and excludes the pairs on which the current idea factors take identical values. The
selected pairs are ranked by acc0(𝑝, 𝑝′) · 𝑤(𝑝, 𝑝′), where 𝑤(𝑝, 𝑝′) = 1.5 if the two programs come from
the same generation and 1 otherwise. The null accuracy acc0(𝑝, 𝑝′) is the fraction of 500 random
permutations of the scores over programs, under which a ranker refit on the permuted labels still
predicts the true order of the pair. A pair with a high null accuracy is easy to order from the idea
factors, so that its misranking indicates a missing idea factor. The null accuracy uses the differences
of the idea factors without the code-length covariate. Up to ℓ= 6 pairs are used, with each program
appearing in at most two pairs. If fewer than 3 pairs are available, the discovery round is skipped.
When the idea memory is empty, ExpEvolve selects the ℓpairs with the largest score gaps under
34


--- Page 35 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
the same constraints (lines 1–2).
Proposing candidates. For each selected pair, the prompt of the proposer LLM contains the score
gap in raw units and in units of 𝜎𝑌, the scores, the predicted scores and the residuals of both programs,
the order predicted by the ranker, the idea factors on which the two programs differ, and the source
code of both programs truncated to 1500 characters each. The proposer LLM is asked to explain the
unexpected order, and proposes 8 candidates in each round, each with a name, a description, a type,
a value set, and a predicted direction (line 6).
Annotation and admission. Each candidate is annotated on the whole archive (line 8). ExpEvolve
admits a candidate if the two values compared by its score contrast are each taken by at least 𝑛min = 5
programs, the absolute score contrast is at least 𝜂= max(0.25 𝜎𝑌, 10−3), and the candidate does not
duplicate an idea factor in the memory, an idea factor removed before, or another selected candidate
(line 9). Two idea factors are considered duplicates if their names are identical, the token Jaccard
similarity of their names is at least 0.6, or the token overlap of their descriptions is at least 0.45.
Since the archive is collected adaptively by the search, the score contrast is an association within the
archive and does not identify the effect of the idea factor. Admission therefore makes an idea factor
available for testing, and the search examines it through the actions (Appendix H.3).
H.3. Idea-Guided Actions
Actions. Allocate compiles the idea factors into actions, i.e., ADD(𝑧) and REMOVE(𝑧) for a binary
idea factor, and SET(𝑧=𝑣) for each value 𝑣of a categorical idea factor (Alg. 1, line 3). The action set
is rebuilt in every generation, and keeps at most three actions of the idea factors with the largest
absolute score contrasts, together with a baseline action without instruction. An action that has stayed
in the action set for 𝑁rot consecutive generations is rotated out to give way to other actions, and its
records are kept for when it enters the action set again. Before an admitted idea factor is compiled
into actions, its absolute score contrast must exceed the 95th percentile of a null distribution obtained
from 200 permutations of the scores, and a threshold on the absolute score contrast is used instead
when the permutation test cannot be run. Background idea factors (Appendix H.4) are not compiled
into actions, until they satisfy the admission conditions of Appendix H.2 and are promoted to regular
idea factors.
Prompt of an action. An idea-guided slot differs from random exploration in two parts of the
prompt (line 5). First, a strategy instruction asks the mutator LLM to use or avoid the pattern of 𝑧, or
to set 𝑧to 𝑣, with the description of 𝑧and its estimated effect. Second, the example programs consist
of the best program in the archive as an anchor, followed by the best programs in the target state of
the action, where ties between programs with similar scores are broken in favor of programs with
rare combinations of idea factors, and 𝑘= 3 example programs are used in total. There is no explicit
parent program, since SCS conditions the mutator LLM on a set of example programs.
Random exploration. A random exploration slot uses the prompt of SCS without strategy
instruction, with 3 example programs sampled uniformly at random from the successful programs,
and the summary of the idea memory.
Diversification in the warm-up. In the warm-up generations, the slots of the baseline action in
the second half of each generation receive a diversification instruction, which asks the mutator LLM
to first list three to five distinct families of well-established approaches to the task as code comments,
and to note which families the example programs use.
Allocating slots. In each generation, Allocate assigns max(2, round(𝜌𝐵)) slots to random
exploration, and the remaining slots to idea-guided actions, where 𝑢𝑡,𝑏denotes the action of slot 𝑏and
35


--- Page 36 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
𝑢𝑡,𝑏= ⊥denotes random exploration (line 3). An idea-guided slot falls back to random exploration if
no action is available, e.g., before any idea factor is admitted, or if the actions have reached the limit
of slots per generation. The fraction of random exploration is thus at least 𝜌.
Bandit. The bandit selects the actions of idea-guided slots with a soft UCB rule,
𝑠(𝑎) = ˜𝑟max(𝑎) + 𝑐
√︄
ln(𝑁tot + 1)
𝑛𝑎
,
Pr(𝑎) ∝exp ␀𝑠(𝑎)
,
where 𝑛𝑎is the number of times that 𝑎has been selected, 𝑁tot = Í
𝑎𝑛𝑎, and 𝑐= 1. Actions that
have not been selected are tried first. The value ˜𝑟max(𝑎) is the maximum reward of 𝑎, minus a
bootstrap estimate of the expected maximum of 𝑛𝑎rewards drawn from all actions, which corrects the
growth of the maximum with the number of samples. The reward of a program generated under an
action follows the normalized reward in Sec. 4.2, where the standard deviation is lower bounded as
𝜎rand = max ␀std(𝑦rand), 0.05 |¯𝑦rand|, 10−6 (line 8). If fewer than two random exploration programs
are available in the generation, the adjacent generations are included. A failed program receives a
penalty score below the worst successful program.
H.4. Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus
Entering and leaving a plateau. ExpEvolve records the best-so-far score at the end of each
generation, and the search is in a plateau if the best-so-far scores of the last 𝜅+ 1 generations are
equal up to a relative tolerance of 10−4, after the warm-up generations. When the search enters a
plateau, ReviseAtPlateau runs the background probe and the dependency judge below (Alg. 1,
lines 12–13). The plateau ends as soon as the best-so-far score improves, and all the changes during
the plateau are reverted in the same generation. Each time the search enters a plateau again, the
probe and the judge are run again, since the background of a new plateau can differ from the previous
one.
Background probe. An LLM reads the 8 successful programs with the highest scores, with the
source code truncated to 1500 characters and the names of the current idea factors, and proposes 2
to 4 binary properties that these programs share. Each property is annotated on the archive, and is
recorded as a background idea factor if at least 5 of the 8 top programs are annotated and at least
80% of them realize the property. A background idea factor stays in the memory after the plateau,
and is promoted to a regular idea factor once enough programs without it appear in the archive and
its score contrast passes the admission threshold.
Dependency judge. The background is described by the three idea factors with the largest
absolute score contrasts. For each idea factor in the memory, and for each value of a categorical idea
factor, an LLM judge decides, with three calls, whether it depends on the background, i.e., loses its
meaning or reverses its effect once the defining property of the background no longer holds.
Changes during a plateau. While the search is in a plateau, ExpEvolve applies the following
changes.
• Reversing and masking actions. For a binary idea factor judged dependent, ADD(𝑧) is replaced
by REMOVE(𝑧) in the action set, with the same description and score contrast, so that the
bandit can only move away from 𝑧. For a categorical idea factor, the actions of the values judged
dependent are masked, while the other values are kept as escape actions. The dependent idea
factors are also removed from the summary of the idea memory. After the plateau, the original
actions are restored, and the records of the reversed and masked actions are kept.

• Stall note. A note on the current state is prepended to the prompt of every slot. The note reports
the best score and the number of generations without improvement, lists the dependent idea
factors with their names and shortened descriptions, states that the search has stalled on this
combination, and asks whether other constructions or combinations can reach a higher score.
• More random exploration. Each idea-guided slot is reassigned to random exploration with
probability 0.9. Since the judge runs at the end of the first plateau generation, the probability
is lowered to 0.3 from the next generation.
• Diversified demonstrations. Random exploration uses the best program of the background as the
first example, and fills the other examples with programs outside the background, which are
selected greedily to diversify their idea factors. A program is considered in the background if it
realizes any dependent idea factor.
• Exploration of the bandit. In the first 2 generations of a plateau, the bandit selects the actions by
the exploration bonus only.

Uncertainty inequality. For a function 𝑔, let 𝐴(𝑔) = inf{𝑟> 0 : 𝑔(𝑥) ≥0 for all |𝑥| ≥𝑟}. For

𝐻0, 𝐻4, 𝐻8, 𝐻12 with 3 free coefficients. The sign conditions are checked on a grid of 2 × 105 points in

and each evaluation is limited to 300 seconds. Since the reformulation enlarges the search space,

implementation, the score is 𝑟2/(2𝜋), where 𝑟is the largest root at which 𝑓changes sign.

Max–min distance ratio. The task places 16 points in the plane to minimize the squared ratio
between the maximum and the minimum pairwise distances. For example, the squared ratios 12.889
and 13.0 in Table 1 correspond to the ratios 3.5902 and 3.6056.
Heilbronn problem for triangles. The task places 11 points in the equilateral triangle with
vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), and (1/2,

Kissing number in 11 dimensions. A set of points 𝐶⊂ℝ11 with 0 ∉𝐶and min𝑥≠𝑦∥𝑥−𝑦∥≥
max𝑥∥𝑥∥over 𝑥, 𝑦∈𝐶yields a kissing configuration of |𝐶| unit spheres. The task constructs such a
set, and the score is the number of points |𝐶|. The distances and norms are only used to check the
validity of the configuration, and a configuration with more points than the known upper bound 868
is rejected.
Circle packing. The task places 26 non-overlapping circles in the unit square to maximize the
sum of their radii. The evaluator checks the non-overlap and the containment of all circles, including
that every radius is at most 0.5 and every center lies in the unit square, and checks that the sum of
radii reported by the program agrees with the radii up to a relative and absolute tolerance of 10−3.
Circle packing via linear programming. A variant of circle packing where the program proposes
only the 26 centers 𝐶𝑖∈[0, 1]2, and the radii are recovered by a linear program that maximizes Í

with the HiGHS solver of SciPy.
Hadamard matrix. The task constructs a matrix 𝐻∈{±1}29×29 that maximizes | det(𝐻)|/(228 ·
712 · 342). Following the convention of Wang et al. (2026), the best-known construction with
| det(𝐻)| = 228 · 712 · 320 scores 320/342 ≈0.9357.
I.2. Baselines
SCS. We use the implementation of SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which generates each program from
a prompt containing the task instruction and 3 example programs sampled uniformly at random
without replacement from the archive. SCS does not maintain an idea memory, and its prompt does
not contain the summary of the idea memory used by ExpEvolve.
SCS+meta. SCS+meta adds the meta-summary of ShinkaEvolve to the prompt of SCS, i.e.,
a textual summary of the insights of recent programs with at most 5 recommendations, which is
rewritten by DeepSeek-V4-Flash at temperature 0 after every generation, without the idea memory, the
idea-guided actions, and the exploration at plateaus of ExpEvolve. It is run on First autocorrelation,
Heilbronn, and Kissing with 10 generations of 20 programs, and on Uncertainty inequality with 20
generations of 10 programs.
ShinkaEvolve. We run ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026) with 5 islands and migration every
10 generations, weighted parent sampling, an archive of 40 programs, a meta-summary every 10
generations with 5 recommendations, and both diff-based and full rewrites. ShinkaEvolve generates
one program per generation, and does not distinguish the two configurations of ExpEvolve and
SCS.
39


--- Page 40 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
I.3. Budget and Resources
All methods evaluate each generated program once, and a failed program consumes the budget. The
LLM calls of ExpEvolve for proposing, annotating, probing, and judging idea factors do not evaluate
programs and do not consume the budget. Each run of ShinkaEvolve starts from 5 copies of the
initial program, one for each island, and then generates 199 programs, so its final performance is
reported at 199 generated programs. The evaluations of ExpEvolve and SCS are not limited in
CPUs, while the runs of ShinkaEvolve on First autocorrelation, Second autocorrelation, Kissing,
and Max–min distance ratio evaluate each program with at most 8 CPUs. The LLM is accessed either
through the official API of DeepSeek or through OpenRouter, depending on the time of the run.
J. Additional Results
Per-seed results. Tables 5 and 6 report the final best score of each seed for the cells of Table 1, and
Tables 7 and 8 report the best-so-far scores along the budget.
Sample efficiency. For each setting, 𝑛ExpEvolve is the first number of evaluated programs at which
the best-so-far score of ExpEvolve, averaged over the seeds that have produced a successful program,
reaches the final best score of SCS averaged over seeds, and 𝑛SCS is the first number of evaluated
programs at which the best-so-far score of SCS, averaged in the same way, reaches its final value.
The programs within a generation are ordered by their slots. Table 9 reports the four tasks in Fig. 6.

11.1
STRATEGY (this batch is targeting a categorical code factor): SET the
‘{feature_name}‘ factor to value ‘{level}‘{ ({desc})}. Past data shows
programs with this exact level gain {+}{ate:.3f} {conf_metric_name} vs
other levels of the factor. The first example below is the highest-Y
program (anchor); the other examples USE this exact level. Adopt the
‘{level}‘ setting and improve on the anchor.
Stall note. At plateaus, the following note is prepended to the prompt of every slot, where {blur}
lists the dependent idea factors as their names followed by the first 90 characters of their descriptions,
separated by semicolons, and {stall} is “best has stayed at {best} for {streak} generations”.
CURRENT-STATE NOTE (read first): the most common combination among the
current top programs is: {blur}. Progress with this combination has
stalled — {stall}. Consider: are there OTHER constructions or
combinations, or variants of the current one, that could reach higher?
If you know one, this attempt is a good moment to try it.
Annotator. The annotator LLM labels the idea factors of a program with the following prompt,
where the descriptions are truncated to 200 characters and the source code to 4000 characters.
[system]
You annotate program code for the presence of specific algorithmic
factors. Output STRICT JSON only with key ’assignments’.
[user]
Factors to annotate:
- <name> (binary): <description>
- <name> (categorical, values: [...]): <description>
Program code:
‘‘‘python
<code>
‘‘‘
Output JSON: { "assignments": { "<factor_name>": <value>, ... } }
For binary factors, value should be true or false. For categorical,
value should be one of the listed values. Use null only if unknown.
Background probe. At the entry of a plateau, the background probe reads the 8 successful
programs with the highest scores, with the source code truncated to 1500 characters, and the names
of the current idea factors.
