These are the TOP-SCORING programs of a search that has plateaued —
they are the stuck family.
## Program {i} ({metric}={score}):
‘‘‘
{code}
‘‘‘
...
Factors already tracked (do NOT repeat these or trivial rephrasings):
- {name}
...
Name the structural / algorithmic properties that these top programs
SHARE — especially the construction or representation they all rely
on. These will be used to describe the stuck family so the search can
deliberately depart from it. Binary properties only.
Return ONLY a JSON array: [{"name":"<snake_case>","description":
"<one sentence, concrete>"}] (2 to 4 entries)
K.1. More Details of Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering
We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to machine learning engineering
(MLE). We integrate its idea discovery and search control into OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) and
evaluate the resulting agent on MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a). This setting examines the use of idea
factors within a harness that supports evolution on ML algorithms towards a specific task objective.
Tasks and data. MLS-Bench evaluates agents on improving components of ML algorithms under
fixed task interfaces and evaluation protocols. Here we consider 6 tasks: Online bandit, Anomaly
detection, Clustering, Multi-objective optimization, Subgroup calibration shift, and Evolution strategy.
Search leverages the scores and execution feedback exposed by each task.
Backbone and budget. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which organizes search
through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators. For each task, we retain a fixed
history containing 20 completed search slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline
and OpenRSI equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50 additional evaluator
calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search slots per generation. All program generation uses
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve.
Integrating idea factors with OpenRSI. ExpEvolve initializes its idea memory from the shared
history and updates it with newly evaluated programs. Consistent with Sec. 4, Discovery examines
program pairs whose score differences are insufficiently explained by the current factors. The LLM
reads their source and proposes reusable mechanisms. Factors 𝑧enter the action catalog when both
states have sufficient support and exhibit a score contrast in the archive. Each generation reserves
two slots for Open exploration and schedules three for Guided search. Specifically, A guided slot
first selects an action, such as ADD(𝑧) or REMOVE(𝑧), and then the harness selects a high-scoring
parent compatible with that change. We use improvement over the best selected parent as action
feedback, adapting the reward reference to OpenRSI’s parent–child structure. When the cumulative
best score remains unchanged within relative tolerance 10−4 across three generation boundaries,
ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration at plateaus, aligning with Sec. 4.2.
Evaluation and results. We evaluate search performance using the best-so-far (BSF) score. For
each task and method, we average the final BSF score over three seeds, starting from the same
20-slot history and continuing for 50 additional evaluations. Fig. 9(a) compares OpenRSI with
OpenRSI+ExpEvolve across the six tasks. The reported configurations improve the mean final BSF
score on all six tasks, with the largest gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.
45


--- Page 46 ---
ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
Ethics Statement
This work studies evolutionary coding agents on open-ended mathematical discovery tasks and on
machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. It does not involve human subjects or personally identifiable
information, and all tasks come from public benchmarks or prior work.
Reproducibility Statement
The full procedure of ExpEvolve is given in Alg. 1 and Alg. 2, and its implementation details and
hyperparameters are given in Appendix H and Table 3. The tasks, evaluators, and reference values
are described in Appendix I.1, the configurations of the baselines in Appendix I.2, the budget and
resources in Appendix I.3, the setting of MLS-Bench in Appendix K.1, and all prompts in Appendix K.
The per-seed results are given in Appendix J. The formal statements and proofs of the theoretical
results are given in Appendix E and Appendix F. All experiments on mathematical discovery use
DeepSeek-V4-Flash unless stated otherwise, and each setting is run with 3 seeds.
AI Use Statement
We used LLM assistance to revise the manuscript’s organization and wording, identify and check
related references, and examine the interpretation of reported experiments. The proposed framework
itself uses LLMs to generate programs, propose idea factors, and assess program properties.
46
